title: Nexus
author: Yuval Noah Harari
blurb: Harari asks why humans, after collecting so much information, still act so unwisely. He argues that information is mainly a way to connect people, not a way to represent the truth. Stories, holy books and bureaucratic documents let millions of strangers cooperate, but they can bind people around fictions and delusions just as easily as around facts. What separates healthy networks from dangerous ones is whether they have strong self-correcting mechanisms, such as independent courts, a free press and scientific institutions. He reads democracies and dictatorships as two different kinds of information network. He then argues that AI is something new. It is not just a tool but an agent that can make decisions and create ideas on its own. That forces us to build institutions able to catch and fix its mistakes before they spread.

lessons.b: The naive belief that more information automatically leads to truth and wisdom is wrong, and history shows why.

lessons.t: Information Connects More Than It Informs
lessons.b: Information's main job is to link people into networks, so a story can be powerful without being true.
Shared stories and bureaucratic records let huge numbers of strangers cooperate, creating realities like nations and money.
issues: scene 4: The dashed connectors from the book to the two right-column group boxes run horizontally through the narrow gap between the top and bottom rows. They hug and touch the box borders and end ambiguously at box edges, so it is unclear which box each line reaches and the lines read as overlapping the boxes. (fix: Route each connector to the left-centre edge of its own box (fan out from the book like scene 1), or move the right-column boxes so their connectors approach from outside the inter-row gap. Leave at least 12px clearance from other box borders and end each line with a clear terminal at its target box.)

lessons.t: The Dream of an Infallible Source
lessons.b: Attempts to bypass human error with holy books or perfect authorities fail, because someone must always interpret them.
Networks that can admit and fix their own mistakes, like science, outperform those that cannot, like the systems behind the witch hunts.
Democracies spread information through many independent channels while dictatorships centralize it, and this shapes how each handles errors.
issues: scene 6: The 'MAJORITY RULE' icon is an empty rounded rectangle with a small bar on top. It reads as a blank frame or broken drawing, not a ballot box, so the left side of the scene does not illustrate anything. (fix: Make it a clear ballot box: add a visible slot and a ballot card half-inserted. Or replace it with a raised-hands or vote-tally graphic tied to the 'MOST VOTES WIN' dots above.)

scene 5: The 'WHAT WAS HAPPENING' label sits under the x-axis at the bottom right. It reads as an axis label instead of naming the falling indigo curve, so the contrast between the two lines is unclear. (fix: Move the 'WHAT WAS HAPPENING' label next to the end of the indigo curve, above the axis, mirroring how 'WHAT THE CENTER HEARD' labels the dashed amber line.)

lessons.t: AI: A New Member of the Network
lessons.b: AI is an agent that makes its own decisions, so our survival depends on building strong self-correcting institutions around it.
